title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 16-20
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-20 of the hermes-consultant series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: How should estimation be understood for agent work?
options: As a prediction of exactly how many hours an entire project will take to finish
As a sizing decision about whether the work fits one window and can be proven
As a firm commitment to a delivery date that the team must then defend
As an average of how long similar tasks happened to take in the past
questions.explanation: Estimation is a decision about how you will work now, not a forecast you cannot control, so you optimize for a shape of work you can finish.

questions.question: Why does a small task ship more reliably than a large one?
options: Because a small task does not need to be verified once it has been finished
Because a small task can safely be handed to a less experienced worker
Because the whole result fits in view, so it can be finished and verified
Because a large task is always more valuable and therefore justifies the extra effort
questions.explanation: A task small enough to see whole can be finished and verified, which is what lets you truthfully report it as done.

questions.question: How should a large goal be decomposed into tasks?
options: Slice by activity, such as writing the tests first and then the code and the docs
Slice by convenience, doing the easiest work first so that momentum builds early
Slice by file, giving one separate task to every file that the change will touch
Slice by deliverable, test each slice against the window, and order by risk
questions.explanation: Splitting by what you produce rather than what you are doing gives slices a client could accept, and risk-first ordering makes a surprise cheap.

questions.question: Why should a skill's description name the situation it applies to rather than just its topic?
options: It is displayed to the client as the title of the deliverable
It is the only part loaded when relevance is decided
It determines which model tier the skill's work runs on
It stores the credentials the skill needs at run time
questions.explanation: Only the description is loaded at the moment relevance is decided, so naming the situation earns the skill a chance to load.

questions.question: How should a reusable skill treat the details that belong to a single client?
options: Inline real names and keys so the steps read concretely
Store credentials in the file so the skill is self-contained
Keep secrets out by name and settings in configuration
Fork the skill per client and edit in their specifics
questions.explanation: The transferable procedure stays client-neutral: secrets are referenced by name and client specifics live in configuration, so the asset travels.

questions.question: What belongs in the body of a skill?
options: An ordered procedure with its pitfalls and checks
A narrative of the incident with dates and ticket numbers
A transcript of how the tool first failed during discovery
A list of every client the procedure has been used for
questions.explanation: Skills hold rules rather than logs: a general rule plus a short why, attached to the step it affects and stated once.

questions.question: What separates a completed handover from a system that is merely finished and delivered?
options: A named client team member owns it going forward
A complete record of every build step is written into a wiki
A final walkthrough is presented to the client's stakeholders
The system has passed one last round of acceptance testing
questions.explanation: Handover is the transfer of ownership, so it is complete when a real person on the client's team is accountable for running and changing the system.

questions.question: Which document does a client reach for when a routine job fails overnight?
options: The reproduce document describing how the system was installed
The decision record of alternatives considered and rejected
The operate runbook that gives steps to keep the system alive
The list of known limits the system deliberately does not handle
questions.explanation: The operate doc is procedural and is the one opened in an emergency; the reproduce doc is the least-used of the three.

questions.question: How is a handover known to be complete?
options: When the documentation covers installation, operation, and evolution
When a client team member runs it from the documents alone
When the credentials have been moved into the client's accounts
When the support window has formally ended on the agreed date
questions.explanation: A handover is verified the way a build is: once a client team member runs the system from the documents without asking a question.

questions.question: What is the difference between change and adoption?
options: Change is what the client pays for; adoption is what the consultant delivers
Change is how the system works; adoption is how people behave in using it
Change is a technical task; adoption is a training session
Change is measured in features; adoption is measured in meetings held
questions.explanation: Shipping the technical change and changing people's behavior are separate outcomes; a system nobody uses is change without adoption, which is a cost rather than value.

questions.question: What does user resistance usually indicate?
options: That the users lack sufficient training on the new system
That the manager has not mandated the tool strongly enough
That a concern about fit or trust was not answered
That the tool needs more features before people will try it
questions.explanation: Resistance is information: it points to an unanswered question about whether the change fits the user's work or can be trusted.

questions.question: Which arrangement best supports adoption sticking?
options: An owner who removes obstacles plus a champion with the pain
A senior sponsor who mandates the tool by memo to the whole team
A company-wide training program delivered to every affected user
A feature-rich release announced before anyone has used the tool
questions.explanation: Authority unblocks a tool while credibility spreads it, so adoption needs both the owner and a champion with real skin in the game.

questions.question: What distinguishes a guardrail from a policy rule?
options: A guardrail is written in more precise legal language than a rule
A guardrail is reviewed by the client while a rule is written by the agent
A guardrail is optional while a rule is mandatory
A guardrail is enforced by the platform regardless of the agent
questions.explanation: A guardrail does not rely on the agent choosing to behave; it mechanically refuses, which is what makes it hold under unattended operation.

questions.question: How should an agent handle personal data?
options: Give the agent all available context so its answers are more accurate
Hold the minimum the work needs and retrieve the rest on demand
Copy full records into its persistent memory for faster reuse
Store records in an external memory service without asking the client
questions.explanation: The safest personal data is the data you do not hold: keep only what the work needs, retrieve the rest on demand, and keep raw records out of persistent memory.

questions.question: What is the default for a dangerous command in an unattended run?
options: Auto-approve it so the unattended job never stalls
Prompt the client each time the command appears
Deny it so the unattended agent is blocked
Route it to the agent to judge whether it is safe
questions.explanation: The deny default keeps a recurring agent from silently picking up destructive commands when nobody is watching; it is a governance decision to keep.
